en: "Kaṭhas, O forest-dwellers! They yoke; the Brāhmaṇas yoke. With these words, he offers an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire. For by means of the mind Prajāpati extended the sacrifice; first by speech, and then by action. Thus the sacrificer, having extended the sacrifice by means of the mind, performs it first by speech and then by action. "Under the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the two spades. Impelled by Savitṛ, he thus takes them up by means of the deities. He takes up four; for there are four quarters, and from the quarters the Pravargya is collected.

He gathers the Pravargya from the very quarters. They are made of wood; for by means of trees indeed is the Pravargya gathered. Verily, by means of trees he gathers the Pravargya. "Arise, O Brahmanaspati!"—with these words he rises. Brahmanaspati is indeed Bṛhaspati. Having become Bṛhaspati himself, he rises. "May the Maruts, the givers of good gifts, come near!"—the Maruts, the givers of good gifts, are indeed the wild animals. In the forest, the Pravargya is gathered.

In the forest itself he makes the forest; with the words, "May Brahmanaspati come forth," he establishes himself. Brahmanaspati is indeed Bṛhaspati; having become Bṛhaspati, he establishes himself. With the words, "May the divine Sūnṛtā come hither," [he proceeds]. The divine Sūnṛtā is indeed Speech; by means of Speech the Pravargya is prepared. Thus, by means of Speech itself, he prepares the Pravargya. With the words, "Toward the hero, manly, whose gifts are fivefold," [he proceeds]. The sacrifice is indeed the hero, the manly one, whose gifts are fivefold.

He gathers the sacrifice for the gods alone. "O divine Heaven and Earth, at the place of sacrifice for the gods, may you both approve of me," he says; for these two were afraid of the Mahāvīra as it was being gathered, thinking, "It will burn us with its brilliance. Bṛhaspati said to them, "This shall be your portion. Thereupon they gave their consent to him. "May I prosper today through the Truth, the head of Makha," he says as he gathers it; thus he gathers the very head of the sacrifice. He carries it three times, for the gods are characterized by the number three.

He encloses [the altar] on all sides with a wooden screen to drive away the *rakṣases*. When Prajāpati was desiring to emit creatures, his vital energy (*tejas*) that was fit for sacrifice departed from him; it entered this earth. Having become a boar, he found it. "It was right here," he said. In that there is earth dug up by a boar, he gathers for himself that very vital energy of the earth which is fit for sacrifice. "O divine ants, you are the first-born of this being"—for the ants are indeed the first-born of this being.

They indeed know this: that which is the living, sacrificial part of this [earth]. When he gathers the anthill-clay, he gathers the very living, sacrificial part of this [earth]. When Indra slew Vṛtra, his vital energy and heroism departed; it entered the plants, and they became the *pūtīka* herbs. "Thou art the vital energy of Indra," [he says]; when he gathers the *pūtīkas*, he gathers the very vital energy and heroism of Indra. "Thou art the body of Prajāpati," [with these words] they milk the she-goat.

The goat is indeed the beloved body of Prajāpati; when they milk the goat, he thereby gathers for himself the beloved body of Prajāpati. (13) With the words, "May honey make you sweet," he pours water upon it; he thus mixes sweetness with sweetness, and it becomes savory. (14) With the words, "Thou art the head of Makha," he takes up the lump of dough; Makha is indeed the sacrifice; he thus restores the head of the sacrifice. (15) With the words, "Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice," he presses down [the two balls].

He places [the fire] on the very foot of the sacrifice with [the formula], "Thou art Gāyatra" (16). He lays down the first *ādhi*. The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor and the Brahman; verily, he bestows splendor and the Brahman upon the sacrificer (17). With [the formula], "Thou art Traiṣṭubha," he lays down the second *ādhi*. The Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor and strength; verily, he bestows vigor and strength upon the sacrificer (18). With [the formula], "Thou art Jāgata," he lays down the third *ādhi*. The Jagatī is indeed cattle.

He places cattle in the sacrificer. With "Thou art Makha," he makes him indeed Makha. With "Thou art the girdle of Makha," he makes it a girdle. Makha is indeed the sacrifice; verily, he makes it for the sake of the sacrifice. It is a span in measure; for the mouth is just this much. Agni is the mouth of the gods; it is commensurate with the mouth from above, for the satisfaction of the deities. He is satisfied with offspring and cattle; the drinking of Soma approaches him.

"He who knows thus"—21. "With the heat of the sun, be heated," he says as he places it in the sunlight; verily, he heats it with the brilliance of yonder Āditya. He sets it down each time earlier [to the west]; verily, he ascends these very worlds. 22. "Thou art the offspring of the bull, belonging to Prajāpati," he says as he speaks over the horse-hairs; for the horse belongs to Prajāpati. Verily, he endows it with its own form. 23. "Let the wives of the gods fumigate thee with the offspring of the bull, the horse," he says as he fumigates it with horse-hairs. 24. For the horse belongs to Prajāpati.

"Prajāpati [performed] the sacrifice for the sake of having a common womb. (24) "For the flame thee, for the radiance thee, for the heat thee"—with these words he places a *śamī* branch on the fire. The fire is indeed brilliance, and the *śamī* branches are brilliance; thus he bestows brilliance upon brilliance. (25) "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people"—with this verse he worships [the fire]. He thereby makes it belong to Mitra. (26) "May the god Savitṛ dig thee up"—with this verse belonging to Savitṛ he digs it up, for the sake of impulsion. (27) "Unwavering on the earth, fill the regions and the quarters."

"Therefore Agni shines in all directions. (28) "Arise, O great one; stand upright! You are firm," he says. Verily, he makes him firm. (29) "Here I endow so-and-so, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman, with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*)," [he says] regarding the Brāhmaṇa. Splendor is indeed the *brahman*, the Gāyatrī.

Verily, he endows him with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). (30) If he should practice sorcery, [he should say]: "This one, the son of such-a-man and such-a-woman, I deprive of splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge. For the *gāyatrī* is indeed splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge; verily, he deprives him of splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge. (31) [He should say]: "This one, the son of such-a-man and such-a-woman, I endow with vigor (*ojas*) and heroism (*vīrya*)," [thus] for a Kṣatriya. For the *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor and heroism.

Verily, he endows him with vigor and strength. (32) If he should practice sorcery, [he says]: "Here, I deprive so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, the offspring of such-a-one, of vigor and strength. For the *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor and strength; verily, he deprives him of vigor and strength. (33) [He says]: "Here, I endow so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, the offspring of such-a-one, with nourishment and cattle. Cattle are indeed the *jagatī*; [verily, he endows him with cattle]. (34)

Verily, he causes him to prosper with vigor and with cattle. (34) If he should practice sorcery, [he says]: "Here, I deprive so-and-so, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman, of vigor and of cattle. Cattle are indeed the moving world; verily, he deprives him of vigor and of cattle. (35) [He says]: "Here, I cause you to prosper with splendor, with holy luster, with vitality, with heroism, with offspring, with cattle, and with food. The self, indeed, is holy luster.

He causes his very self to prosper with that brilliance, with sacred luster, with vital energy, with heroism, with offspring, with cattle, and with food. (36) "For the upright one, thee! For the virtuous one, thee! For a good dwelling, thee!"—thus, according to the sacrificial formula, he sets down each subsequent [brick] after the previous one; he thus descends toward these very worlds. (37) "With the eye of the sun, I gaze upon thee"—with these words he looks down. For if he were to look at this [world] with the eye of men, his eye would be consumed, and offspring would be born blind.

He looks upon it with the eye of the sun itself. "May speech moisten you," he says; he moistens it with milk. Speech is indeed the Gāyatrī; verily, by means of speech he moistens it. "May vigor moisten you," he says; vigor is indeed food; verily, by means of food he moistens it. "May milk moisten you," he says; milk is indeed cattle.

"Verily, he hardens him with animals: 'May the essence harden thee! May the oblation harden thee! May Soma harden thee! May the sacrifice harden thee! May the *brahman* harden thee! May Prajāpati harden thee!'—according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). 'O *Brahman*, we shall proceed with the *pravargya*,' the Adhvaryu addresses the *Brahman*. At this time, the sacrifice rests in the *Brahman*; therefore he says to him, 'The *yajus*-equipped [sacrifice]'—thus says the *Brahman*."

This sacrifice is indeed the chariot of the *Yajus*; the Adhvaryu yokes it at the sacrifice. That is why the Adhvaryu is called "Adhvaryu. The Adhvaryu leads it forward; the Adhvaryu is the leader of this entire [sacrifice]. The Adhvaryu directs the other priests, saying, "Do this, do that"—this is what he means by saying this. (49) "Let them be anointed with the *Sāmans" means that the *Sāmans* themselves are its two wheels on both sides. (50) "Brought together with all thoughts" means that the sacrifice is indeed brought together with all thoughts.

With all the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*) indeed does the sacrificer prepare the sacrifice—[as it is said]: "The extended one, who carries [the sacrificer] across. By saying "the extended one, who carries across," he means "by means of the sacrificial gifts. "Let the *stobhas* carry [the sacrifice], being well-disposed. The *stobhas* are indeed the *hotṛ*-priests; they indeed carry the sacrifice at this time. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om! This, indeed, is the truth of speech; that which is the truth of speech.

Therefore, he proceeds with it together [with Indra]. (55) "Proceeding with Indra," [he says] for the sake of being accompanied by Indra. (57) "With the eastern quarter, with Agni as the deity, with the Gāyatrī metre, I enter the spring season"—thus they enter from the front toward the east and the spring, so that there may be no burning. (58) "With the southern quarter, with Indra as the deity, with the Triṣṭubh metre, I enter the summer season."

"By the southern quarter, with Savitṛ as the deity, and by the Jagatī metre, I enter the summer season"—thus one enters the southern quarter and the summer from the south, so that there may be no burning. "By the western quarter, with Savitṛ as the deity, and by the Jagatī metre, I enter the rainy season"—thus one enters the western quarter and the rains from behind, so that there may be no burning. "By the northern quarter, with Mitra and Varuṇa as the deities, and by the Anuṣṭubh metre, I enter the autumn season."

"By the northern direction and with Bṛhaspati as the deity, by the *pāṅkta* metre, I enter the winter season"—thus they enter the upward direction and the cold from above for the sake of non-burning. "By this direction and with Prajāpati as the deity, by the *anāpta* metre, I enter the cool season"—thus they enter this [direction] and the cool season from it for the sake of non-burning. "I enter the *gāyatrī* metre."

"Brahman is indeed splendor, and the Gāyatrī is splendor; they enter into splendor itself so as not to be consumed. (64) "I enter the Triṣṭubh metre," he says. The Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor and strength; they enter into vigor itself so as not to be consumed. (65) "I enter the Jagatī metre," he says. The Jagatī is indeed cattle; they enter into cattle themselves so as not to be consumed. (66) "I enter the Anuṣṭubh metre," he says. The Anuṣṭubh is indeed speech.

"Into speech itself I enter, for the sake of non-burning. The fivefold hymn-form (*paṅkti*) is indeed the sacrifice; thus they enter the sacrifice for the sake of non-burning. "Into the *atiśchandas* meter I enter"—the *atiśchandas* meters are indeed the meters; thus they enter the meters for the sake of non-burning. "Into the meters I enter"—the meters are indeed cattle; thus they enter cattle for the sake of non-burning. "May these carry us across."

"May they protect us"—thus he invokes a blessing. "May he who hates us and whom we hate meet with them"—he thus afflicts with pain the one whom he hates. "May the waters enter us; may the waters watch over us"—the waters are all the deities; he thus causes the deities to enter [him] so that there may be no burning. "May I attain life, all-life, universal life; may I attain full life"—this is what he says.

He who knows thus attains a full lifespan; moreover, he makes the year and the quarters a protective armor on every side. With the formula, "For Yama thee, for Makha thee," he sprinkles the Mahāvīra. Makha is indeed the sacrifice; it is for the sake of the sacrifice that he sprinkles it. The Pratiprasthātṛ spreads out the sprinkled [materials]. They proceed with the rite: "O divine leader, may you be worthy of honor; may you be worthy of heaven. With the Veda-grass-bundle, he cleanses the Mahāvīra; then he cleanses it three times.

For the gods are true to the three [truths]. He cleanses it on all sides; he thereby makes this [vessel] pure and fit for sacrifice on every side. "Protect it from contact with the earth! Thus he draws a silver plate beneath it. Indeed, these worlds were afraid when the *mahāvīra* was being cast forth, thinking, "He will consume us all with his brilliance. They ran to Prajāpati for refuge. That Prajāpati said to the Earth, "Become silver and support the *mahāvīra*."

He said to the intermediate space, "I shall conceal you with the lords of the forest. He said to the sky, "Becoming green, protect the Mahāvīra from above. Therefore, one draws silver beneath it, so that the earth shall not be scorched. [With the words] "Thou art flame; thou art radiance," he carries the blazing fire for the sake of its brilliance. [With the words] "They anoint him," he joins the principal Mahāvīra to it. Agni is indeed brilliance, and the Mahāvīra is brilliance.

"He places luster into luster itself. [He offers with: "Svāhā to the out-breath! Svāhā to the diffused breath! Svāhā to the in-breath! — He employs the Mahāvīra vessel for the Gharma. Indeed, when the Mahāvīra was being employed, the quarters were afraid of it, thinking, "It will burn us all away with its luster. They ran to Prajāpati for refuge. Prajāpati said to them, "It will burn you bit by bit; I shall interpose the deities between you and it."

"Therefore, he measures out the directions by a span: 'Unassailable in the east, under the overlordship of Agni'—he thus places Agni in front as a protection against burning. 'Grant me long life,' he says; thereby he invokes this blessing for himself. 'Rich in offspring in the south, under the overlordship of Indra'—he thus places Indra in the south as a protection against burning. 'Grant me progeny,' he says; thereby he invokes this blessing for himself. 'A good seat in the west, under the overlordship of the god Savitṛ'..."

He places Savitṛ behind as a barrier to prevent burning. With the words, "Give me sight," he invokes this blessing for himself. The subsequent layer is the Āśruti, under the overlordship of Mitra and Varuṇa; he places Mitra and Varuṇa above as a barrier to prevent burning. With the words, "Give me hearing," he invokes this blessing for himself. The uppermost layer is the Vidhṛti, under the overlordship of Bṛhaspati.

He places Bṛhaspati above [the Mahāvīra] for the sake of preventing its burning. With the words, "Grant me speech," he invokes this blessing upon himself. Saying "Svāhā," he encloses it from all sides. For that sun is Rudra, the Mahāvīra, and the Maruts are indeed the rays; thus he encloses it with the rays themselves. With the words, "Thou art the partition of the atmosphere," he places a fuel-stick on top.

He places [the cover] over [the vessel] with pieces of wood (*vanaspati*) for protection. 90 With the formula, "May you touch the heaven," he covers it with a green [leaf], so that the heaven may not be scorched. 91 "Worthy, you carry arrows and a bow; worthy, you wear the worshipful, multiform golden ornament (*niṣka*). Worthy, you bestow all this power; O Rudra, there is nothing more mighty than you. With these words, he indeed arouses his majesty. 92 "You are the *gāyatra* [meter]; you are the *traiṣṭubha* [meter]; you are the *jāgata* [meter]"—with these words, he hands it to the *pratiprasthātṛ*. For the officiants are the *hotṛ*s.

He thus bestows him upon the *hotṛ*-priests. One [portion] goes to the *āgnīdhra* and one to the *pratiprasthātṛ*. They walk around to the right, shaking [the vessel] while saying, "Honey! Honey! Honey!"—by this he says, "I shall collect the honey of the bees. [Saying] "Thou art out-breath (*prāṇa*), thou art diffused-breath (*vyāna*), thou art in-breath (*apāna*)," he places those very breaths—the out-breath, the diffused-breath, and the in-breath—into the sacrificer. [Saying] "Thou art hearing (*śrotra*)," he places hearing itself into the sacrificer. All the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) surround [him]; for the officiating priests are indeed the *hotṛ*-priests.

He thus unites him with the *hotrās*. With the verses beginning, "May Agni shake thee," he shakes him by means of these very deities. When [the fire] has been kindled, he takes up the gold plate (*rukmam*) with the verse: "The celestial Gandharva, the lord of the world..."—the "world" (*bhuvanam*) here refers to these worlds; he is their overlord, who is Rudra... "the one to be invoked by the mind among the people... "I entreat thee, O God, the divine, with a prayer (*brahman*). For if they were to attend upon him with a mere prayer (*brahman*), it would injure him.

Brahman is auspicious and peaceful; he thus attends upon him with Brahman itself. (He says,) "In heaven is thy seat"; by this he means, "In heaven is thy home. "In heaven, O worshipful one, thou art backed, sun-skinned"; for when Rudra had gone to the heavenly world, the gods did not recognize him as he moved about, radiant as the sun. They said, "Who are you? He replied, "I am Rudra, I am Indra, I am Āditya, I am the devourer of all through my divine power. They said, "Expel him! He spoke to them in response.

He ran toward them. They said, "You are everything (*sarva*). Because he spoke what is called *rudra*, that is the *rudratva* (the nature of Rudra) of Rudra; because [they said] "you are" (*bhavān*), that is the *bhavatva* (the nature of Bhava) of Bhava; because [they said] "everything" (*sarva*), that is the *śarvatva* (the nature of Śarva) of Śarva. He became auspicious (*śiva*). That is the *śivatva* (the nature of Śiva) of Śiva. He dissolved into them. That is the *mṛlatva* (the nature of Mṛla) of Mṛla. The gods said to him, "Sovereignty over the past, the present, and the future (*bhūta*, *bhavya*)."

"It leads the sacrificer to sovereignty over all" (100). "With the blameless ones, with the united ones," he says. The *hotrā*s are indeed the blameless ones; with them this [sacrificer] is joined in the *pravargya* rite. By means of those very ones, he causes him to attain the *pravargya*. "The ocean, they say, is their seat" (101). The Vedas are indeed the oceans.

He unites him with those very [rays] during the Pravargya rite: "O lightning of the thunderbolt, O lightning of the stars, you who accompany Viśvāvasu the Gandharva—to them let there be homage; may they be gracious to us, may they grant us protection. Whomsoever we hate and whosoever hates us, him we place within their jaws. "I have seen the herdsman, never resting"—this is the Sun; he is the guardian of the worlds.

"He does not rest by night nor by day, moving along the paths hither and thither"—therefore he traverses all paths, whether they be to the south or to the north. "Clothing himself in those that meet and those that diverge"—for there are four directions that meet for him and four that diverge.

Wearing these [garments], he indeed envelops these worlds with brilliance. (103) "Here you have shone forth for the two lovers of honey, honey for the two who seek honey"—by saying this, when [he says] "the Gharma has been made radiant," he means, "I shall collect the honeyed Gharma. (104–105) "Agni has united with Agni; he shines together with the god Savitṛ, together with Sūrya—Svāhā! At this point, Agni indeed unites with Agni at this very moment. (107) "Agni has united with fervor; he has shone together with the god Savitṛ, together with Sūrya. (108)

"The upholder of heaven shines across the mid-region; the upholder of the vast atmosphere, the upholder of the earth—the immortal god, born of fervor, the upholder of the gods. Indeed, yonder sun sustains these worlds with his splendor. "For the heart thee, for the mind thee, for the sky thee, for Sūrya thee"—verily, he causes him to go to yonder world. "This sacrifice upward"—the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; [he says this] for the sake of the sacrifice's upward ascent. "May the *hotrā* offerings reach the gods in heaven."

"By the *hotrā*s... (111). "The embryo of the gods, the father of prayers, the lord of creatures"—for he is indeed the embryo of the gods, the father of prayers, and the lord of creatures. "Grant us life; you are the Gharma, the giver of splendor; you are our father, know us as your children"—with these words, he invokes this blessing for himself (112). "Homage be to you; do not harm me"—this is for his own safety (113). "May we serve you together with Tvaṣṭṛ"—for from him these creatures are born; it is for procreation, for the sacrifice indeed... (114).

The head was cut off. Now, at that time, the Aśvins were the physicians of the gods who did not drink the *gharma*. The gods said to them, "You two are indeed physicians; restore this head of the sacrifice. They replied, "Let us choose a boon: let the *pravargya* belong to us alone. The gods said, "You have indeed encompassed everything; let it be ours as well in this matter. They replied, "Let it be milked for us first; let it be offered for us first."

Therefore, of these two alone, [milk] is first milked and first offered; for water and ghee are their [share]. They restored the head of the sacrifice. Thereupon, what blood flowed forth became the *udumbara* tree. In that the vessels are made of *udumbara* wood, he places vigor (*ūrj*) into the sacrifice itself. What was its sap became the *muñja* grass; therefore they make the sacrificial cord (*veda*) from *muñja* grass. [He] invokes the purifier... [he] calls out.

"Come hither!"—with these words he indeed calls her from heaven. "Come hither!"—with these words he indeed calls her from the intermediate space. "Come hither!"—with these words he indeed calls her from the earth. The Vedas are her udders, and the *brahman* is her calf. By means of the *brahman* as the calf, the gods milked out speech, cattle, and immortality. Whoever knows the secret names of the Vedas reaches a full lifespan; he becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*), he becomes firmly established, and he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food.

"Mayobhūreko vasuvidekassudatra eko viśvapoṣyekaḥ"—these indeed are the secret names of the Vedas. He who knows this attains a full lifespan, becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*), finds firm support, and becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. (117) "O Sarasvatī, that breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is the source of bliss, which bestows jewels, which is the finder of wealth, and by which you nourish all desirable things—that one, here, for the sake of suckling... with these words he consecrates [the breast]. (118) "Thou art the turban of Aditi," [he says].

Having bound her to the tethering post, he makes her truly well-vowed. With the words, "May Pūṣan [lead] thee," he lets the calf loose for the sake of its staying with the mother. With the words, "Be eager for the Gharma," he turns it away.

One who intends to perform the Pravargya rite on the following day should, on the preceding day, set aside the two Vatsārkara vessels for the Gharma. Likewise, having released the two milk-cows in the morning or evening, if the cow that yields the Gharma-milk should perish, one should then milk the vow-cow (vratadhenu) instead. From that [cow], one should milk the half-vow Gharma, using two teats at a time. Here, if the cow that yields the Gharma-vow perishes, the twice-born should proceed with clarified butter (ājya). If goats perish, however, he should use the milk of a cow, or else bring another cow. If all [the animals] perish, he should bring milk that has been curdled with clarified butter, or simply milk, or curds. 48. They milk the cow.

If one were to milk this [cow] with the haste of a camel, he would spill it; when they milk the she-goat, it is the *gharma* itself that he spills. Indeed, he spills strength when they milk the she-goat; thus they gather strength for the *gharma*. Therefore they say: "Come hither with a share of strength, O Indra and Aśvins! Drink the honeyed *sāragha* *gharma*, O Vasus! Sacrifice, O Vala! He pours the strength into the *mahāvīra*.

"Verily, he brings together strength in the cauldron (gharma). 122 He consecrates the [ladle] as it moves upward with the formula: "To the ray of the sun, for the pouring of rain, svāhā! Whatever oblation indeed rises from here, from that very place it causes rain to fall. By this very oblation, he pours down rain from the sky. 123 "Thou art Gāyatra; thou art Triṣṭubh," [with these words] he takes up the two hoof-pieces. 124 "Thou art Jagatī," [with these words] he takes up the base-ring (upayāma).

Verily, he encloses it with the meters. "I enclose thee with heaven and earth," [saying this] he encloses the *mahāvīra* with the two hooves; for these two are indeed the hooves. Verily, by means of these two he encloses it. "With the intermediate space I support thee," [saying this] he holds it from below with a supporting base (*upayāma*). Moreover, the supporting base is indeed the intermediate space.

He indeed supports it in the intermediate space. "With the permission of the gods and the ancestors, may I be able to carry you," [he says]. He offers with the formula, "To Rudra, svāhā! To Vāta, svāhā! If he were to offer according to the sacrificial verse (*yajus*), he would consign the cattle to Rudra; he would be without cattle. He should merely recite the sacrificial verse. Thus Rudra avoids the cattle. At this time, all these deities are longing for him, thinking, "He will offer to me! He will offer to me!"

The deities themselves were intent upon him; they were capable of harming him if he were without their share. When he says, "To Agni, accompanied by the Vasus, svāhā! he provides a share for the deities so that they may not harm him. Some deities have a share in the *yajus* (the sacrificial formula), while others have a share in the *āhuti* (the oblation).

He gratifies both of these [worlds]. "Place this sacrifice in heaven, place this sacrifice in heaven"—these worlds and the quarters indeed desired companionship in the *gharma*. When he says, "Go to heaven, go to the sky, go to the earth, go to the five directions," he thus satisfies these very worlds and the quarters in the *gharma*. "Go to the gods who drink the *gharma*."

He thus satiates with the *gharma* those very gods who drink the *gharma*. With the formula, "To the gods who drink the *gharma*, svāhā! he offers into the *mahāvīra* with the *upayāma* ladle. He thus satiates with the *gharma* those very gods who drink the *gharma*. The gods and the Asuras performed the *pravargya* rite to exactly the same extent. Whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too. Those Asuras proceeded with the *pravargya* in a low voice; it consumed them. The gods proceeded with the *pravargya* in a loud voice.

Those gods became [prosperous] and the Asuras were defeated. ... [The sacrificer] offers the second [portion]. That indeed becomes an offering made for his own self, accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call. (133) "O Aśvins, drink the Gharma," says the sacrificer; thereby he asks for satisfaction. Moreover, it becomes accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call. (134) "May all directions be seated on the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," with these words the Brahman priest consecrates the offering; that indeed becomes an offering made for his own self. (135) "Swell for nourishment (*iṣ*), swell for strength (*ūrj*)!"—thereby he bestows nourishment and strength upon the sacrifice.

"Swell for this *brahman*, swell for this *kṣatra*, swell for this people (*viś*)," he says; thus he makes the *brahman*, the *kṣatra*, and the people partakers. "Swell for this sacrificer who presses [the Soma]," he says; thus he invokes this blessing for the sacrificer himself. "Swell for well-being," he says; thus he attains prosperity. "Swell for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," he says.

“He becomes possessed of Brahman-splendor. (139) “For me, for long life, for splendor, for preeminence, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny—overflow! With these words, he invokes this very blessing for himself. (140) “For brilliance thee! For glory thee! For prosperity thee! For power thee! With these words, he moves the vessel clockwise. He thereby makes the quarters partakers [of the offering], for his own safety. (141) “Thou art Dharma, O Sudharman; uphold these sacred formulations (brahmans) for him!”—Agni, indeed, is Rudra.

Just as one cuts portions for Agni, so too does he perform this Agnihotra rite with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, the oblation is offered; honey is the oblation; to Indra, to Agni, svāhā! This is indeed the conclusion, having the form of heaven. Moreover, he offers mentally to Prajāpati to avoid interruption, for Prajāpati is like the mind, and the sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati; thus he maintains the continuity of the sacrifice. They deliberate: "Should he consume it, or should he not?"

If he were to eat [the remains], he would become a *prākāruka* (one who causes discord); if he were not to eat, he would be without strength. He should smell it; thus he accomplishes both. The sacrificer alone eats; he thereby bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon himself. (143) "Recite for the one being settled," he says, for the sake of stability. (144) "For the day thee! For Sūrya thee! For the night thee! For the constellations thee!"—thus he makes the day and night, as well as the sun and the constellations, sharers in the sacrifice. The *Brāhmaṇa* mantras of the *Yujate* section are concluded.

"O Gharma-jaṭhara and Annāda Brāhmaṇas, make me an eater of food among this people; may I become an eater of food among this people. Indra and Agni are indeed the Gharma-jaṭhara and Annāda among the gods. They are the masters of food. They bestow food upon him. He becomes an eater of food who knows thus. "O Kavi and Mātariśvan, make me possessed of nourishment among this people; may I become possessed of nourishment among this people. Kavi and Mātariśvan are indeed [the masters] among the gods.

Those two are the lords of nourishment; they bestow nourishment upon him. He who knows this becomes possessed of nourishment. (VS 14.7) "O you two who have the sun as your seat, grant sight to me among this people; may I be possessed of sight among this people. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed the gods whose seat is the sun among the deities; they are the lords of sight. They bestow sight upon him.

"He who knows thus becomes possessed of sight. (147-1) "O Father and Mother, make me possessed of hearing among this people; may I be possessed of hearing among this people," [he says]. Heaven and Earth are indeed the Father and Mother of the gods; they have mastery over hearing. They bestow hearing upon him. He who knows thus becomes possessed of hearing. (148) "O Yama and Aṅgirasa, make me long-lived among this people; may I be long-lived among this people," [he says].

Yama and Varuṇa, the two Aṅgirases among the gods—they are the lords of life. May they bestow life upon us. He who knows this becomes long-lived. (149) "May we partake of your Gharma, which is honeyed and full of nourishment; homage be unto you; do not harm me"—this is for the sake of non-injury to oneself. (150) "You are the light of the trees, the essence"—with these words he first fills it with honey. Honey, indeed, is the essence of the flowers and fruits of the trees. By that very means, he causes it to prosper.

Regarding this, it is said: "Life is indeed honey. [If one were to say,] "He would place life into the fire; he would be liable to die," [therefore he says]. When he says, "Place life in me," he places life in himself and becomes long-lived. "Light is your portion, the essence of the waters and plants"—with ghee he performs the second [offering]. This is indeed its beloved abode; by that very means he prospers him. When he says, "Place sight in me," he places sight in himself and becomes possessed of sight. ... [With curd] he performs the third [offering].

This indeed is his beloved abode; by that very means he causes him to prosper. When he says, "Bestow vigor upon me," he thereby places vigor within himself; he becomes vigorous. "Fierce and shaker"—this is a group of verses to be recited in the forest for the sake of peace. "O Agni, lord of vows! O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Sūrya, lord of vows!"—these indeed are the lords of vows among the gods.

Having announced this to them, he undergoes the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). (155) "The earth is the fuel," according to the sacrificial formula (*yathāyajuḥ*). (156) "May the day be pleased with its banner; may the beautiful light [be pleased] with light, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the *rauhiṇa* oblation. Yonder sun is indeed the banner of the days. (157) "May the night be pleased with its banner; may the beautiful light [be pleased] with light, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the *rauhiṇa* oblation. The moon is indeed the banner of the nights. These two, the sun and the moon, are the eyes of the Pravargya.

"The two eyes are the Rauhiṇas; verily he bestows sight upon the eyes. (158) "Homage to Rudra who dwells in heaven, whose arrows are the rain," for when it rains fiercely, he strikes down creatures by making the rain his arrow. (159) "Homage to him"—thus he makes the rain auspicious. (160) "With him may I meet"—by this he means, "May I not encounter him in a narrow place. (161) "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space, whose arrows are the wind. (162) Thus he says.

When he blows fiercely, he indeed strikes down creatures by making the wind his arrows. "Homage to him!"—thus he makes the wind auspicious. "May I not contend with that one"—by this he means, "May I not encounter him in a narrow place. "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth, whose arrows are food"—when he [blows] fiercely, he indeed strikes down creatures by making food his arrows. "Homage to him!"—thus he makes food auspicious. "May I not contend with that one"—by this he means, "May I not encounter him in a narrow place."

"The *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants"—with these very praises he praises him. When [the teacher] says, "O Brahman, listen to me, *bhūḥ*! he bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon himself. Therefore, one should not perform the *pravargya* rite for one who is not learned in the Vedas; for at that time, such a person is not one who has heard the Veda. [The teacher says], "May we here be sharers of the most abundant portion. He thus makes him a partaker of the Vedas themselves.

Therefore they say: "The Adhvaryu indeed knows the sacrifice; the Adhvaryu becomes the leader of the others. (VS 33.74) "The tawny bull has bellowed, great like Mitra, beautiful to behold. For were he to heat the creatures while becoming Varuṇa, no one would be left remaining. Rather, having become Mitra, he heats the creatures. (VS 33.75) "He has shone together with Sūrya. Indeed, the radiance of him for whom this [fire] is kindled becomes like that of Sūrya.

"Indeed, all these deities are now waiting upon the curd-mixture (dadhigharma) of the Adhvaryu, thinking, 'He will take [the portion] for me; he will take it for me. If he were not to take [it], those deities would look toward him with intent, and being without their share, they might harm him. When he takes [it] with these two [formulas] addressed to all the deities—'For Indra whomsoever,' and 'For as many [deities]'—he makes the deities sharers, so that there may be no injury to himself. He who knows thus attains a full lifespan. He offers five oblations with the formula, "To Pūṣan the glowing, svāhā! etc.

Pūṣan is indeed Rudra; Rudra is Āghṛṇi. These are the fierce names of Rudra. When one is about to perform the removal (*udvāsana*), one thereby makes atonement to all the deities. He who knows this attains a full lifespan. (173) "O Gharma, that heat of thine which is in heaven, which is in the *jagatī* metre, which is in the seventeenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), and which is in the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*)—I appease those [heats] for thee; svāhā!"

Verily, by this he expiates for Rudra from that very Jagatī metre, from the seventeenfold Stoma, and from the Havirdhāna cart. He who knows thus attains a full span of life. "O Gharma, that heat of thine which is in the intermediate space, which is in the Triṣṭubh metre, which is in the fifteenfold Stoma, and which is in the Āgnīdhra—those I appease for thee; Svāhā! Verily, by this he expiates for Rudra from the intermediate space, from the Triṣṭubh metre, from the fifteenfold Stoma, and from the Āgnīdhra fire-shed.

"He who knows thus attains a full lifespan. (175) "O Gharma, that heat of thine which is on the earth, which is in the Gāyatrī metre, which is in the Trivṛt-stoma, which is in the Sadas—by this [offering] I have appeased it; Svāhā to it! By this, he truly expiates the Rudra-element from this very earth, from the Gāyatrī metre, from the Trivṛt-stoma, and from the Sadas.

"He who knows thus attains a full lifespan" (176). He offers the oblation with the verse, "Anumati has approved for us today," once [the fire] is established. Anumati is indeed this earth; she is the foundation. Thus he establishes himself upon her. He first fills [the ladle] with honey; this is its beloved abode. By that very means, he causes it to prosper. With the words, "Come hither, O Agni... they lead him forward. This is indeed the world of the gods; they lead him up toward the world of the gods.

They lead the wife forward for the sake of non-shattering; he covers the wife with a garment. The garment indeed belongs to all the deities; verily, he causes her to prosper through all those deities. He gives the command for the Sāman. This is his singing along;

moreover, they thus humble themselves before him as they proceed, saying: "Protect me from the highest heaven; protect my body from the mid-region; by the law of the earth we follow thee for new-found prosperity. By this he says, "Do not harm these worlds. "Protect my breath," he says; verily, he invokes this blessing upon himself.

"On the way, they take a second [step] and proceed, saying: 'O Brahman, protect us from the beyond; guard the body of the Kṣatra; we follow you, O Viś, according to the Law (dharman), for new prosperity. By this he says, 'Do not harm our offspring,' and 'Protect my out-breath.'"

He invokes this very blessing for himself. Having reached the third [layer], they approach and proceed with the formula: "Protect my breath from the highest; protect the body of my sight; by the law of my hearing, we follow after thee for new prosperity. By this he says, "Do not harm my vital breaths. With the words, "Protect my downward breath," he invokes this very blessing for himself. These become the *vedas*. He thereby makes these [hair-like strands] into hair. On both sides are the potsherds (*kapāla*); he thereby makes them into potsherds.

On both sides he places two gold plates; he thereby forms the two eyes. Behind [the gold plates] he places the pot for the cooked rice (carusthālī); he thereby forms the mouth. Behind [the pot] he places the dipping-spoon (sruva); he thereby forms the neck. On both sides [of the neck] he places the two hoof-shapes (śapha); he thereby forms the two shoulders (aṃsau). He makes the two offering-spoons (sruc) the two arms, for the sake of wholeness. On both sides there are two fans (dhavitra); he thereby forms the two ribs. In the middle is the base-ring (upayāma) and the two cords, which are made of bamboo; he thereby forms the belly.

He places two teeth from the upper lip at the back; he thereby forms the thighs. On both sides there are cross-bars; he thereby forms the shanks and the thighs. He places two fire-stirring sticks on both sides; he thereby forms the feet. In the middle he places the fan; he thereby forms the navel. Above he places the seat; he thereby forms the chest. He covers it with a black antelope skin; for the black antelope skin is the form of the Brahman; verily, he covers him with the Brahman.

He covers it with *muñja* grass. *Muñja* is indeed strength; verily, he covers it with strength. He mixes it with curds for the sake of brilliance; thus Rudra does not strike him down. He makes it with *haṃsa*-grass. Yonder sun is indeed *haṃsa*; that is his form. He goes around sprinkling [water] with the words, "Thou art auspicious, the bestower of vigor. Verily, he thereby bestows vigor upon him. With the words, "A child, the sustainer of men," he proclaims his very form and his greatness.

If he should think, "These creatures will worship this *dharma* as they do birds," he should know that he must protect [the fire] from birds. He should offer oblations with the two verses, "With mouth of blood, go forth like a cow" and "Do thou bear [it] hither and do thou bear [it] around. *Yama* is indeed death; by means of his own portion, he pacifies him. With the verse, "Bear [it] happily and bear [it] around," he invokes a blessing. With the verse, "May the waters be friendly to us," they pour out water.

"Sumitrā indeed makes them so," [he says]. "May they be Durmitrās for him," [he says]; he should pour [the water] toward that direction in which his enemy may be. "He thus makes them Durmitrās. "This is your food, O Gharma; this is your soil," [he says]. Ghee is indeed curd; honey is the food of this [earth].

"By that very [means] he causes him to prosper. (190) "By that do thou increase"—by means of food, he causes him to prosper. (192) "May we increase and may we swell"—he thus invokes a blessing. (193) "Thou art named Ranti"—this indeed is the auspicious name of Rudra. Thus, he invokes this blessing for himself. (194) "Indu, Dakṣa, Śyena, Ṛtāvā, Hiraṇyapakṣas—come after my drinking of Soma; be fuel, may we be fueled"—thus they appease Rudra. (195–196) "Come after my drinking of Soma; be fuel, may we be fueled"—thus they appease Rudra.

They do not afflict him with pain. With the words, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper," he invokes a blessing. With the words, "Place splendor in me," he bestows splendor upon himself. He offers ten oblations with the verse, "Upwards that Jātavedas... The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food; thus he becomes firmly established in the Virāj, which is the enjoyment of food. They ask: "What does one gain by the consecration (dīkṣā), and what by the intermediate consecration (avāntara-dīkṣā)? One gains the self through the consecration, and the progeny through the intermediate consecration.

He who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) remains consecrated for twelve years; for him, this intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*) serves as his formal initiation. He ties on a girdle, he takes up a staff, he brings fuel-sticks, and he brings them again. They are made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is indeed strength (*ūrj*); verily, he bestows strength upon the student. They are made of *parṇa* wood; the *parṇa* is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); verily, he bestows spiritual luster upon the student.

They are made of *śamī* wood. The *śamī* is indeed brilliance; verily, he places brilliance within the student. "O Agni, lord of vows, the earth is the fuel," with these words he offers the first fuel-stick. Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods on earth. Having informed him [of his vow], he performs the vow; he becomes one who observes the vow. "O Vāyu, lord of vows, the atmosphere is the fuel," with these words he offers the second fuel-stick. Vāyu is indeed the lord of vows among the gods in the atmosphere.

Having announced it to him alone, he performs the vow; he becomes one who observes the vow (vratya). With the words, "O Sūrya, lord of vows, may heaven be the fuel," he places the third fuel-stick. Sūrya is indeed the lord of vows among the gods in yonder world. Having announced it to him alone, he performs the vow; he becomes one who observes the vow. He does not speak aloud, nor does he look about; thus he bestows splendor upon himself. He should stand during the joint of the moon and sit during the day, remaining at night for the sake of possessing splendor; he eats food that is cooked by fire and by the sun.

The consecrated one is indeed the sacrificial oblation; he eats only the oblation. He recites [the invitatory verse] when the rite is completed. He who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) falls away from the other worlds. When he places fuel-sticks upwards from here, by that he becomes established in yonder world. When he places them downwards from yonder, by that he becomes established in this world. He should recite [the invitatory verse] when a boar emerges from the womb; he should recite it when a bull eats barley; he should recite it when a pig eats lotus-fibers.

He recites only for the sake of the perfection of form. Indeed, he who is a religious student (brahmacārī) is deprived of splendor, progeny, cattle, sacred luster (brahmavarcasa), and food. When he does not speak out nor look upon [the fire], he places splendor within himself. When he speaks out to and looks upon a maiden, he places progeny within himself. When he speaks out to and looks upon a calf, he places cattle within himself. When he speaks out to and looks upon the sun, he places sacred luster within himself.

When he utters or looks upon the milk-rice (*kṣīraudana*), he places food within himself. Moreover, he who knows this becomes radiant, possessed of offspring, cattle, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). "O giver of life, give me life"—thus they place life within themselves. ... Having placed [the bricks] while being consecrated, he purifies them.

The givers of breath [say], "Give me breath," and they place breath within themselves. The givers of out-breath [say], "Give me out-breath," and they place out-breath within themselves. The givers of in-breath [say], "Give me in-breath," and they place in-breath within themselves. The givers of sight [say], "Give me sight," and they place sight within themselves. The givers of hearing [say], "Give me hearing," and they place hearing within themselves. The givers of luster [say], "Give me luster," and they place luster within themselves. For our long life...

"Give back the body"—thus they place life-breath itself within themselves. "For non-slipping, for non-burning; obeisance to the Rudras. Indeed, the gods excluded Rudra from the sacrifice. He stood grasping his bow. Indra, in the form of an ant, cut the bowstring. He let out a roar (*ghṛṅ*). His pain crushed his head. That became the *pravargya* rite. Because he was a great deity possessing heroic power, it is called the *mahāvīra*. Because he let out a roar (*ghṛṅ*) with his bow, it is called the *gharma*.

Because it is brought forth (*pra-vṛjyate*), it is called *pravargya*. Therefore, he who sacrifices with the *sapravargya* sacrifice places the head of Rudra upon himself. Rudra does not strike him down, provided he knows thus. These indeed are the *śukriya* [chants] of the *śukriyas*; that is the reason for the *śukriya*-nature of the *śukriyas*. With these, the gods prepared themselves at the beginning of the sacrifice. Because they prepared themselves (*prāvṛñjata*), they are called *pravargyas*; therefore, it is the *pravargya*.

Therefore, he who sacrifices with the Pravargya rite becomes preeminent and endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). This Jyotiṣṭoma was indeed the sacrifice at that time. Just as other fires are distributed from a fire once it has been produced, so do other sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratu*) spring forth from this one. Therefore, one should perform the Pravargya in the Jyotiṣṭoma for the sake of the upward growth of the sacrifice. One should not perform the Pravargya in the Ukthya; for the Ukthas are indeed offspring and cattle.

If one were to pour [the Mahāvīra vessel] during the Ukthya sacrifice, it would consume his offspring and his cattle. Therefore, one should not pour for one who desires offspring or desires cattle. That sun up there is Rudra, the Mahāvīra; as Rudra, the god, he excludes offspring and cattle. Therefore, one covers the wife with a garment so that her offspring may not be consumed by fire. At the commencement of the entire rite, one should pour [the Mahāvīra], saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Homage to Vāc! Homage to Vācaspati! Vāc is indeed Sarasvatī.

"Salutation to that speech which has been uttered and that which has not been uttered. (208-1) "Salutation to the seers (*ṛṣis*), the makers of mantras, and the knowers of mantras. (208-2) "May the seers, the makers of mantras, and the knowers of mantras not abandon me. (208-3) "I shall utter divine speech"—thus he utters only divine speech. (208-4) "Auspicious and unceasing"—thus he makes it auspicious and unceasing. (209) "Pleasant to the gods"—thus he makes it pleasant to the gods. (210) "Endowed with *svadhā* for the ancestors"—thus...

"By [the formula], 'For the fathers, he makes her full of *svadhā*'; for the fathers, he indeed makes her full of *svadhā*. 'Worthy of service for men'; for men, he indeed makes her worthy of service. 'May the gods favor her for beauty; may the fathers rejoice after her'; the gods indeed favor him for beauty, and the fathers rejoice after him. 'May I be well-eyed with my eyes, well-lustred with my face, and well-hearing with my ears'—this is according to the sacrificial formula."

At the conclusion, they also purify themselves with the mantra: "May Śivā be most auspicious for us; may Sarasvatī be very gracious. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; by means of speech they set out, and by means of speech they proceed. With the formula, "Thou art the underlayer for the Brahman; I spread thee for the Brahman," he provides an underlayer for offspring and cattle. With "Thou art the dwelling-place for Iḷā," it is for the sake of stability. [He recites: "O Vāta, blow hither healing; O Vāta, blow away whatever is evil. Vāyu is indeed breath.

He makes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) his most abundant [portion], with the verse: "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss... and with the words: "The *Ṛg* verses, the *Yajus* formulas, and the *Sāman* chants. For the Veda is indeed threefold; thus, for him, the security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) of his offspring, cattle, and subjects becomes established in a threefold way. Now, when he is about to undertake the vow (*vrata*), having gone to the forest to a pure spot of ground outside the village where no roof-covering is visible, he causes [the student] to recite. Indeed, the village is the stall of Death, whereas the forest belongs to the gods.

He who knows this overcomes repeated death. One should study when the sun has risen, in the forenoon, during the bright fortnight, and during the northern course of the sun; for this is the *triśukriya*. He becomes a possessor of the *triśukriya* who knows this. [One should not study] when there are clouds, nor in a crowd, nor at the edge of a cow-pen, nor on the joints or sub-joints of the year, for the sake of one's own safety. Nor should one study facing a dead person among bipeds or quadrupeds, for the sake of one's own safety.

He does not eat meat from bipeds or quadrupeds that have died. Having seen a Caṇḍāla, an impure person, or other unclean things, he eats these [foods] for the sake of purification. He does not eat on the previous day after having eaten meat. He does not approach unchastity on the previous day. On that very day, in the forenoon, he should not have his hair, beard, body hair, or nails cut; he should not scratch himself, nor apply collyrium, nor anoint himself with oil, nor bathe, so as not to lose his vital energy (*tejas*). He should not come into contact with village animals unless they have been consecrated with a rite of pacification (*śānti*).

He should have the vessels made. The consecration (*dīkṣā*) is indeed austerity; thus, by means of austerity itself, he yokes it for him. He stands to the north. Into that [vessel] he yokes the principal *mahāvīra* pot, and the other two day after day. Of these, the first is *gāyatra*, the second *traiṣṭubha*, and the third *jāgata*. Day after day, he yokes the meters in their proper order. The *pravargya* is indeed the head of the sacrifice.

Its skull-bones are the *kapālas*, its hair the two fans, its ears the handles of the fans, its nostrils the two gold plates, and its eyes the two [plates]. The right [plate] is golden and the left is silver; the *mahāvīra* vessels are its neck, the *carusthālī* its mouth, its jaws the *śaphas*, its ankles the *aniṣṭubdhis*, its knees the *damṣṭras*, and its teeth the *mayūkhas*. When he places it in the *gharma*, that is its tongue; the *payāma* and the ropes are its sinews, and the *purolāśa* is its brain.

When he covers [the altar] with coals, [he says]: "May my hair, the Vedas, clarified butter, marrow, milk, fat, the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, the vital breaths, the *sāman* chants, the lights, the quarters, and the sense of hearing—these indeed constitute the head of the sacrifice. He who knows this becomes preeminent and chief. This, verily, is the head; it does not depart from him. They said to him: "O Blessed One, these two are your eyes; look upon me with them."

The sun and the moon are his two eyes. (219-1) "With this essence, honey, I anoint your form; may I be anointed with that form"—this he says to proclaim the majesty of his very form. "I anoint you with the rites of the gods, with the ointments of the gods; O Blessed One, may you be my name. This, indeed, is the beloved name of Rudra.

With his own dear name he anoints him with the ointments of the gods. "Of thee, those are the *ṛc*s, the *yajus*es, and the *sāmans*"—by saying "the *ṛc*s, the *yajus*es, and the *sāmans*," he says this very thing. "One [eye] in Agni, another in the sun; one in the sun, another in Agni; one in Agni, another in Agni"—thus he stimulates his two eyes. For Bhaga is blind.

"Blind offspring are not born from him. [The sacrificer] says, "May I become possessed of fortune (bhaga)," and thus he bestows sight upon himself. He says, "Thou art the eye; thou art sight; thou art hearing; thou art speech named Purandhi. Thus he instructs him; therefore, instructed offspring are born. He says, "With that by which Śatakratu offered his portion, with that I invoke thee, O Fortune! Indeed, the gods excluded Rudra from their share. He turned back toward the gods with his bowstring drawn.

The gods invoked him by this dear name, the Pravargya; he invokes him by his own dear name. "O heroes, I reveal that fierce deed of yours for the sake of gain, as thunder reveals rain, when Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, with the head of a horse, proclaimed the honeyed secret to you both. Agni rules over the friendship of the Vasus; may Agni grant us those things of great fortune."—Agni indeed is Rudra.

He was Vāsavyasaubhaga... Now, the gods and the Asuras performed the Pravargya ritual equally. Whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too. Those gods saw these openings; with them, they looked down upon this Gharma in the sacrifice when it had been made radiant. Those gods prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated.

When one gazes upon the Pravargya with these openings, he becomes possessed of progeny, possessed of cattle, and worthy of honey. (226) "Ten you shine toward the east, ten toward the south"—this is for the attainment of the quarters. Who indeed knows how many these worlds are? With these openings, he attains all the worlds. (227) "Ten you shine toward the east, ten toward the south, ten toward the west, ten you shine toward the north, ten upward, shining with a well-disposed mind. Luster, indeed, is light.

He thus rouses this very splendor [with the words]: "O thou who art not wrathful, protect our offspring and cattle. This is for the protection of offspring and cattle. He who knows this becomes possessed of offspring and cattle; so too does he who knows the *Pravargyopaniṣad*. The gods were indeed afraid of the glowing Mahāvīra vessel, thinking, "It will consume us all with its splendor. They ran to Prajāpati for refuge.

That Prajāpati said: "Worship him with something else; he will become auspicious. [He replied: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. [Prajāpati said: "He has been placed upon the earth (bhuvaḥ). [He replied: "For strength (nṛmṇāyi), for strength (nṛmṇam). Offspring indeed are strength, and cattle are strength. Thus, he expiates Rudra for both offspring and cattle. He chants the *udgītha* of the Sāman with the words "nidhāyyo vā nidhāyyo vā"; by that very means he establishes himself in the *nidhana*. [He says: "Svar jyotiḥ."

Yonder sun, indeed, is this light. By that very means he causes him to prosper. These are his beloved bodies; by them he causes him to prosper. These are his unexpressed hymns of praise; with them they praise him. These are his expressed hymns of praise, namely, the *svar* and the light; with them they address him directly. These are his unexpressed names: *bhuvas*, *nṛmṇas*, *nidhis*, *svar*, and *jyotis*. It is him they cause to prosper visibly.

This world is indeed the *gārhapatya* fire; that [heavenly] world is the *āhavanīya*. Those who perform the oblation in the *gārhapatya*, then carry it forward and proceed with it in the *āhavanīya*, depart from this world. Having established this [fire] again, they proceed [with the rite], saying: "O Agni, lord of the house... He thus pays homage to the *gārhapatya*; he finds firm support in this very world. This is indeed the womb of the waters; it is for the sake of being born from that womb.

If one who possesses splendor desires, "May I become more splendid; may I become possessed of Brahman-splendor," then for him, having drawn this [milk], he should perform the *Pravargya* at the midday pressing. Splendor indeed is Brahman-splendor, and the *Pravargya* is splendor; verily, he secures for himself splendor and Brahman-splendor. If he should offer it, he should make a fourth lump with the words, "Thou art of the *Anuṣṭubh*. The *Anuṣṭubh* is speech; verily, he yokes speech at the mouth of the sacrifice. He should have the vessels made in two parts.

They should remain there until the Soma-pressing for the sake of freshness; one should place the fire in the Āgnīdhra shed. It should shine forth in the Āgnīdhra, it should be established in the Āgnīdhra, for this is the Āgnīdhra’s own abode; thus, at this very time, he bestows radiance upon him in his own abode. He offers in the Uttaravedi; the Uttaravedi is indeed the heavenly world, [offering there] for the attainment of the heavenly world. In that very spot, prior to the purificatory bath (Avabhṛtha), he collects the vessels. To the south, he places the Āhavanīya fire; he collects the vessels.

He scatters [the earth] toward the Āhavanīya fire; he hides the vessels, or alternatively, they may carry them to an island. Yonder sun is Rudra, the Mahāvīra; he becomes radiant and possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) among men. One should perform the *pravargya* on that day in a multi-day sacrificial session—[but not during the *pravargya* itself]—thereby one secures spiritual luster. [The *pravargya* is performed] during the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifices; during the afternoon of the *varuṇapraghāsa*s; during the morning of the *mahāhavis*; and during the afternoon of the *śunāsīrīya*.

At this very point, before the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), he collects the vessels. He places the *āhavanīya* fire to the south; he collects the vessels; he buries the *āhavanīya* fire to the west; he hides the vessels—or alternatively, they may carry them to an island. "Yonder sun is Rudra, the *mahāvīra*; [thereby] one secures splendor (*varcas*) and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Regarding this, they say: "The spiritual luster of one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice is indeed unsecured. One should perform the *jyotiṣṭoma* together with the *pravargya* rite; thus, one places spiritual luster in its own very source.

He becomes possessed of brahman-splendor; the Udgātṛ sings these *parisāman* chants. He sings them for the success of the *pravargya* rite. There is the *śārṅga*; he sings it while the [milk] is being poured. The *śārṅga* is indeed splendor; verily, by means of splendor, he brings him to fulfillment. There are the *śukra* and *candra*; he sings them over two pieces of gold. The *śukra* is indeed breath, and the *candra* is food; verily, by means of these two, he brings him to fulfillment. There are the two bodies of the *gharma*; he sings over them while they are being heated.

He causes him to prosper by means of his own body. There are two *vratapakṣa* (flanks of the vow). He sings over them as they are being placed upon the fire. Indeed, at this time, the *Rakṣases* strive to consume the entire *gharma*. The *vratapakṣa* are the thunderbolt of *prāmada*; [they serve] for the striking away of the *Rakṣases*. The two *Aśvins* are present in the *vrata*. He sings over them when they have been offered; he thus makes it palatable. This is indeed his singing along (*upagāyana*); moreover, they hum along with him. The two *rājanarauhiṇa* cakes are present. He sings over the two *purolāśa* offerings.

The sun and the moon are indeed the two eyes of the Pravargya; the two Rājanarauhiṇa cups are the eyes. Thus he bestows sight upon the eyes. It belongs to Aṅgiras. He sings this while the Parigharmya vessel is being placed [on the fire]. Verily, the Aṅgirases went from here to the heavenly world; by means of this Sāman, they ascended upwards to the heavenly world.

When the *pravargya* belonging to Aṅgiras has been performed, the world of heaven is ascended; it is for the complete attainment of the world of heaven. Regarding this, they say: "The *gharma* consists of the *Ṛg*, the *Yajuṣ*, and the *Sāman*. For him whose *pravargya* is being performed while they are performing the *pravargya*, they perform it as a whole—possessing strength, possessing its source, and possessing its body—for the sake of prosperity. Through that, the sacrificer attains prosperity.

He prospers in life and vigor whose *mahāvīra* breaks apart. With the verse, "Even without a binding," he should bind it with clay from a ritual site or by means of strengthening it with a firm adhesive (*abhiśriṣ*). If the *mahāvīra*, while being carried forth, should leap out, the sacrificer would become a builder of walls. To prevent this, he should offer two oblations with the verses, "The sky leaped unto the earth," for the sake of non-leaping. He attains a full lifespan; that indeed is the expiation in that case.

The Pravargya of this man is struck down by lightning when it thunders while the Mahāvīra vessel is being heated. That pain seizes the sacrificer. He should offer oblations with the two verses beginning, "When he has roared, Agni has roared. For Agni is indeed the Roarer; thus he pacifies him with his own portion. He attains a full lifespan. This is the expiation in that case. Or rather, the Pravargya of this man is struck by the thunderbolt when it rains while the Mahāvīra vessel is being heated.

That sacrificer becomes long-lived. He should sing this verse to Parjanya; he should offer oblations with the two verses beginning "To Parjanya. Water, indeed, is Parjanya. By means of his own portion, he pacifies him. He attains a full lifespan. That itself is the expiation in that case. Or rather, darkness seizes the sacrifice of him at whose *mahāvīra* the sun sets while it is being heated.

The sacrificer suffers distress. He should offer oblations with the two verses, "Upwards that Jātavedas" and "The bright one of the gods has risen. Indeed, that Āditya is Rudra, the Mahāvīra. By means of his own portion, he pacifies him. He attains a full lifespan. That indeed is the expiation there—that indeed is the expiation there. Verily, Rudra intends harm to the cattle of him for whom a Gharma-drinker sits down while the Mahāvīra is being heated.

"From whatever you sit in fear, from that grant us fearlessness; grant us fearlessness for our cattle; homage to Rudra, the bountiful"—with these two verses he should offer oblations. Agni is indeed Rudra. By means of his own portion, he appeases him and makes him favorable. He attains a full lifespan. This is the expiation in that case.

Death indeed seizes the offspring of him for whom birds or beasts of prey run about while the Mahāvīra is being set forth. He should offer oblations with the two verses beginning, "With mouth of blood, he goes apart like a cow. Yama is indeed death; by means of his own portion, he appeases him, for his own safety. When they are about to proceed with the Pravargya rite for one who has been initiated, he prepares the Pravargya equipment.

He gathers the materials upon a black antelope skin; indeed, Agni gathers them. He [levels it] with pebbles for stability, and with the potsherds for the sake of the earth. There is a stool made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is strength (*ūrj*); verily, he supports them with strength. Its cross-beams are made of Muñja grass; the Muñja is strength; verily, he supports it with strength. Its legs are a span high; by this much, indeed, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) extend; verily, he supports them. He spreads a black antelope skin; he covers [the stool] with a black antelope skin.

The black antelope skin is indeed the form of Brahman; with Brahman itself he supports it. He prepares the mound (khara) to the northeast of the Gārhapatya fire; he makes two further mounds facing north. This world is the Gārhapatya, and yonder world is the Āhavanīya; what is offered in the Gārhapatya causes one to go to the heavenly world. ... Having closed the doors from the outside, he proceeds with the Pravargya rite—for the sake of warding off misfortune and for distinction. "Yonder sun is Rudra, the Mahāvīra"—thus ends the Brāhmaṇa concerning the belly of the Gharma.
Thus ends the Śukriya Brāhmaṇa, [numbered] 240.
